name: zclaw
vibe_summary: An ultra-minimalist OpenClaw-style AI assistant squeezed into 888KiB of firmware running on ESP32 microcontrollers. It brings GPIO control, cron scheduling, and persistent memory to bare-metal hardware with a hacker-friendly C codebase.
best_for: Makers wanting an AI assistant on ESP32 hardware
GPIO and sensor automation via natural language
Learning embedded AI agent architecture in C
avoid_if: You need rich chat-channel integrations beyond Telegram/web relay
You want a mature plugin ecosystem
You are uncomfortable flashing firmware and provisioning devices
You need multi-user or team features
openclaw_advantages: Runs on $5 ESP32 hardware with an 888KiB all-in firmware budget
Direct GPIO, I2C, and DHT sensor control from natural language
Extremely low power footprint for always-on deployments
No desktop OS or server required; fully self-contained firmware
Encrypted credential storage in flash with secure flash mode
openclaw_disadvantages: Far fewer chat channels (Telegram/web relay vs. OpenClaw's broad channel support)
Requires hardware flashing and serial provisioning workflow
Constrained by MCU memory and rate limits for LLM calls
No desktop or mobile app experience
confidence_summary: Strong evidence from README, docs, and recent commits about architecture and features; community sentiment is uncertain due to zero Reddit matches and web results mostly referencing OpenClaw itself rather than zclaw.

overview_markdown:
zclaw is a radically minimal take on the OpenClaw personal-AI-assistant concept, written in C and targeting ESP32 microcontrollers (e.g., Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-C3). The entire firmware — including ESP-IDF/FreeRTOS runtime, Wi-Fi, TLS/crypto, and certificate bundles — is capped at 888KiB, with only ~35KB of application code. Despite the tiny footprint, it supports natural-language chat via Telegram or a hosted web relay, timezone-aware cron-style scheduling (daily, periodic, one-shot), persistent memory, and composable custom tools.

Where OpenClaw runs as a gateway process on desktops and servers bridging many chat platforms, zclaw pushes the assistant to the edge: it can directly drive GPIO pins, read DHT sensors, and talk to I2C hardware, making it a physical-world agent rather than a pure software one. Recent releases (v2.13.0) added DHT and generic I2C hardware tools, hardened tool schemas, and kept firmware size in check, showing active, disciplined maintenance.

Security-conscious touches include encrypted credential storage in flash via a secure flash mode, bootstrap script integrity verification (SHA256), LLM rate limits (100/hour, 1000/day by default), and Telegram chat-ID allowlists. It supports both cloud LLM backends and local models via Ollama, making it a strong fit for privacy-focused, low-power, always-on deployments — at the cost of OpenClaw's rich channel ecosystem and desktop-class capabilities.
